'''Jack Herschel Freed'''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physicists to be Honored at 1997 March Meeting |url=https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/199703/physicists.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250417182530/https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/199703/physicists.cfm |archive-date=2025-04-17 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> (born April 19, 1938) is an [[Americans|American]] chemist known for his pioneering work in [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (aka electron spin resonance) spectroscopy. He is the Frank and Robert Laughlin Professor of Physical Chemistry, emeritus, at [[Cornell University]].

==Biography==
Jack Freed was born in [[New York City]]. He received his bachelor's degree in [[chemical engineering]] in 1958 from [[Yale University]] and his Ph.D. in chemistry in 1962 from [[Columbia University]].

Freed is currently the Frank and Robert Laughlin Professor of Physical Chemistry, emeritus, in the department of chemistry and chemical biology at [[Cornell University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.cornell.edu/jack-freed|title=Jack Freed {{!}} Chemistry & Chemical Biology Cornell Arts & Sciences|website=chemistry.cornell.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06}}</ref> In 2001, Freed founded the National Biomedical Center for Advanced Electron Spin Resonance Technology (ACERT)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://acert.cornell.edu/index_files/acert_personnel.php|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080517112401/http://www.acert.cornell.edu/index_files/acert_personnel.php|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 17, 2008|title=ACERT: Personnel|website=acert.cornell.edu|access-date=2017-07-06}}</ref> funded by [[National Institutes of Health]] and has been its director since then. In 2004, he was an editor for ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry]]''. Before that he was a fellow in numerous places such as [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], [[American Physical Society]], [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]], Hebrew University Institute for Advanced Studies, and [[Weizmann Institute of Science]]. 

In 2023, he received two grants totalling $7.8 million over five years from the National Institutes of Health to use [[Electron paramagnetic resonance|electron-spin resonance]] (ESR) for the benefit of public health. Located in Baker Lab on Cornell’s Ithaca campus, this national resource will provide cutting-edge ESR spectroscopy for biomedical researchers engaged in projects aimed at understanding and combating diseases and ailments. The resource is the only one in the U.S of its kind.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NIH funds Cornell-led biomedical initiatives {{!}} Cornell Chronicle |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2023/08/nih-funds-cornell-led-biomedical-initiatives |access-date=2023-12-13 |website=news.cornell.edu |language=en}}</ref>
